en: 7. Anusaya-yamaka 7.2 Mahāvāra 7.2.5.
Pahīna-vāra (The Chapter on What Has Been Abandoned)

7.2.5.1. Positive Person (Anulomapuggala) For whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) also been abandoned for that person? Yes.
Or conversely, for whom the underlying tendency to aversion has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to sensual lust also been abandoned for that person? Yes.
For whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) also been abandoned for them?

For a non-returner (*anāgāmī*), the underlying tendency to sensual lust has been abandoned, but the underlying tendency to conceit has not been abandoned for them. For an arahant, both the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to conceit have been abandoned.
Or conversely, for whom the underlying tendency to conceit has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to sensual lust also been abandoned for them? Yes, it has.

For whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) … [and] the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) been abandoned? Yes.
Or conversely, for whom the underlying tendency to doubt has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to sensual lust been abandoned?

For two types of persons, the underlying tendency to doubt has been abandoned, but the underlying tendency to sensual lust has not been abandoned. For two other types of persons, both the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to sensual lust have been abandoned.
For whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*)...

[and so on] ...the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) also been abandoned? For a non-returner (*anāgāmī*), the underlying tendency to sensual lust has been abandoned, but the underlying tendency to ignorance has not been abandoned. For an arahant, both the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to ignorance have been abandoned.
Or conversely, for whom the underlying tendency to ignorance has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to sensual lust also been abandoned? Yes, it has.
For whom the underlying tendency to aversion has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to conceit also been abandoned for them?

For a non-returner, the underlying tendency to aversion has been abandoned, but the underlying tendency to conceit has not been abandoned for them. For an arahant, both the underlying tendency to aversion and the underlying tendency to conceit have been abandoned.
Or conversely, for whom the underlying tendency to conceit has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to aversion also been abandoned for them? Yes, it has.

For whom the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) ... [and so on] ... the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) been abandoned? Yes.
Or conversely, for whom the underlying tendency to doubt has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to aversion been abandoned?

For two types of persons, the underlying tendency to doubt has been abandoned, but the underlying tendency to aversion has not been abandoned. For two other types of persons, both the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to aversion have been abandoned.
For whom the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*)...

[and so on] ...the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) been abandoned? For a non-returner (*anāgāmī*), the underlying tendency to aversion has been abandoned, but the underlying tendency to ignorance has not been abandoned. For an arahant, both the underlying tendency to aversion and the underlying tendency to ignorance have been abandoned.
Or conversely, for whom the underlying tendency to ignorance has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to aversion been abandoned? Yes, it has.

For whom the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) ... [and so on] ... the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) been abandoned? Yes.
Or conversely, for whom the underlying tendency to doubt has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to conceit been abandoned?

For three types of persons, the underlying tendency to doubt has been abandoned, but the underlying tendency to conceit has not been abandoned. For an *arhat*, both the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to conceit have been abandoned.
For whom the underlying tendency to conceit has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to lust for existence ... pe ... the underlying tendency to ignorance been abandoned? Yes.
Or else, for whom the underlying tendency to ignorance has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to conceit been abandoned? Yes.
For whom the underlying tendency to views has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to doubt been abandoned? Yes.
Or again, for whom the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) also been abandoned? Yes.

… [as before] … For whom the underlying tendency to doubt has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*) … [and so on] … up to … the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) also been abandoned?

In three types of persons, the underlying tendency to doubt has been abandoned, but the underlying tendency to ignorance has not been abandoned. In the case of the Arahant, both the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to ignorance have been abandoned.
Or again, for whom the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) been abandoned? Yes.
For whom the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*) has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to ignorance been abandoned? Yes.
Or again, for whom the underlying tendency to ignorance has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to lust for existence been abandoned? Yes. (The section based on a single root.)

For whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) have been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) also been abandoned?

For a non-returner (*anāgāmī*), the underlying tendencies to sensual lust and aversion have been abandoned, but the underlying tendency to conceit has not been abandoned. For an arahant, the underlying tendencies to sensual lust and aversion have been abandoned, and the underlying tendency to conceit has also been abandoned.
Or conversely, for whom the underlying tendency to conceit has been abandoned, have the underlying tendencies to sensual lust and aversion also been abandoned? Yes.

For whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion have been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to views... [and so on] ...the underlying tendency to doubt also been abandoned? Yes.
Or conversely, for whom the underlying tendency to doubt has been abandoned, have the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion also been abandoned?
For two types of persons, the underlying tendency to doubt has been abandoned, but for them the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion have not [been abandoned].
And they have been abandoned. For two types of persons, the underlying tendency to doubt has been abandoned, and the underlying tendencies to sensual lust and aversion have also been abandoned.
For one in whom the underlying tendencies to sensual lust and aversion have been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to existence …pe… the underlying tendency to ignorance also been abandoned?

In the case of a non-returner, the underlying tendencies to sensual lust and aversion have been abandoned, but the underlying tendency to ignorance has not been abandoned. In the case of an arahant, the underlying tendencies to sensual lust and aversion have been abandoned, and the underlying tendency to ignorance has also been abandoned.

Or, for one in whom the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) has been abandoned, have the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) also been abandoned? Yes. (The section based on two roots.

For one in whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) have been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) ... pe ... the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) also been abandoned? Yes.

Or, for one in whom the underlying tendency to doubt has been abandoned, have the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit also been abandoned?
In two types of persons, the underlying tendency to doubt has been abandoned, but the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, and conceit have not been abandoned.
In a non-returner, the underlying tendencies to doubt, sensual lust, and aversion have been abandoned, but the underlying tendency to conceit has not been abandoned.
In an arahant, the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to sensual lust [have been abandoned].
And the underlying tendency to aversion and the underlying tendency to conceit are abandoned.

For one in whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit are abandoned, is the underlying tendency to existence ... pe ... the underlying tendency to ignorance abandoned? Yes.

Or, for one in whom the underlying tendency to ignorance is abandoned, are the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit abandoned? Yes. (The Section Based on the Triad.)

For one who has abandoned the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views, has that person abandoned the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.

Or conversely, for one who has abandoned the underlying tendency to doubt, have that person abandoned the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views?
For two types of persons, the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to views have been abandoned, but the underlying tendency to sensual lust has not [been abandoned].

The underlying tendency to aversion and the underlying tendency to conceit have been abandoned. In the non-returner, the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to views have been abandoned, but the underlying tendency to conceit has not been abandoned.

In the arahant, the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit have been abandoned, as well as the underlying tendency to views.
...and abandoned ... [as before] ... (Based on the Fourfold Root.

For one who has abandoned the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt, has that person abandoned the underlying tendency to existence ... [as before] ... the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.

Or conversely, for one who has abandoned the underlying tendency to ignorance, has that person abandoned the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes. (Based on the Fivefold Root.)

For one who has abandoned the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence—has that person abandoned the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.

Or conversely, for one who has abandoned the underlying tendency to ignorance—has that person abandoned the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence? Yes. (The Section Based on the Sixfold Root.
7.2.5.2. Positive Plane (Anuloma-okāsa)
Where the underlying tendency to sensual lust is abandoned, is the underlying tendency to aversion abandoned there?
One cannot say either that it is abandoned or that it is not abandoned.

Or conversely, where the underlying tendency to aversion is abandoned, is the underlying tendency to sensual lust abandoned there? One cannot say either that it is abandoned or that it is not abandoned.
It should not be said that [it] is either "abandoned" or "not abandoned.
Where the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) is abandoned, is the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) abandoned there? Yes.
Or conversely, where the underlying tendency to conceit is abandoned, is the underlying tendency to sensual lust abandoned there?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) is abandoned; however, regarding the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*), it cannot be said to be either "abandoned" or "unabandoned.
In the two feelings of the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*), both the underlying tendency to conceit and the underlying tendency to sensual lust are abandoned.

Wherever the underlying tendency to sensual lust is abandoned, is the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) ... pe ... the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) abandoned there? Yes.
Or again, where the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) also been abandoned there?
In the case of painful feeling, in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and in the formless realm (*arūpadhātu*), the underlying tendency to doubt has been abandoned;

however, regarding the underlying tendency to sensual lust, it cannot be said that it is either "abandoned" or "unabandoned. In the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), within the two types of feeling [pleasant and neutral], the underlying tendency to doubt...

It cannot be said that it has been abandoned, nor can it be said that it has not been abandoned.

It cannot be said that it has been abandoned, nor that it has not been abandoned.

Or again, where the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) also been abandoned there?
In the two feelings of the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*), in the fine-material sphere (*rūpadhātu*), and in the immaterial sphere (*arūpadhātu*), the underlying tendency to doubt has been abandoned;
however, regarding the underlying tendency to aversion, it cannot be said to be either "abandoned" or "unabandoned. In the case of painful feeling (*dukkhā vedanā*), here...
The underlying tendency to doubt has been abandoned, and the underlying tendency to aversion has been abandoned.
Where the underlying tendency to aversion has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to lust for existence there also been abandoned?
It cannot be said that it has been abandoned, nor can it be said that it has not been abandoned.
Or again, where the underlying tendency to lust for existence has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to aversion been abandoned there?
It cannot be said that it has been abandoned, nor that it has not been abandoned.

Or, where the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) also been abandoned there?
In the two feelings of the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*), in the fine-material sphere (*rūpadhātu*), and in the immaterial sphere (*arūpadhātu*), the underlying tendency to ignorance has been abandoned;
however, regarding the underlying tendency to aversion, it cannot be said to be either "abandoned" or "unabandoned. In the feeling of pain (*dukkhā vedanā*), the underlying tendency to ignorance...
Where the underlying tendency to aversion has been abandoned, the underlying tendency to resentment has also been abandoned.
Where the underlying tendency to conceit has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to views... [and so on] ...the underlying tendency to doubt also been abandoned there? Yes.
Or conversely, where the underlying tendency to doubt has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to conceit been abandoned there?
In regard to painful feeling, the underlying tendency to doubt is abandoned here; as for the underlying tendency to conceit, it should not be said to be either "abandoned" or "unabandoned.

In regard to the two feelings within the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), and in regard to the form-sphere realm (rūpadhātu) and the formless-sphere realm (arūpadhātu), both the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to conceit are abandoned.
Where the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*) also been abandoned there?

In the fine-material sphere (*rūpadhātu*) and the immaterial sphere (*arūpadhātu*), both the underlying tendency to conceit and the underlying tendency to lust for existence have been abandoned.
Or rather, where the underlying tendency to lust for existence has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to conceit also been abandoned there? Yes.
Where the underlying tendency to conceit has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to ignorance also been abandoned there? Yes.
Or rather, where the underlying tendency to ignorance has been abandoned, has the underlying tendency to conceit also been abandoned there?

In regard to painful feeling, the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) is abandoned here; as for the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*), it should not be said to be either "abandoned" or "not abandoned.

In regard to the two types of feeling within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), and in regard to the form-sphere realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless-sphere realm (*arūpadhātu*), both the underlying tendency to ignorance and the underlying tendency to conceit are abandoned.

“Abandoned” or “unabandoned. In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, both the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*) are abandoned.

however, regarding the underlying tendencies to sensual lust and aversion, it cannot be said that they are "abandoned" or "not abandoned. In the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*), within two types of feeling, the underlying tendency to conceit...

however, regarding the underlying tendencies to sensual lust and to aversion, it cannot be said that they are either "abandoned" or "not abandoned. In the two feelings of the sense-sphere element, the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to sensual lust are abandoned here;
however, regarding the underlying tendency to aversion, it cannot be said that it is either "abandoned" or "not abandoned."
Or: In unpleasant feeling, the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to aversion are abandoned;
however, regarding the underlying tendency to sensual lust, it should not be said that it is either "abandoned" or "unabandoned.

Is it the case that wherever the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion are abandoned, there the underlying tendency to existence is also abandoned? No, there is not.
